intro.lead: I'm a high-school senior in New Jersey. I write Rust tools for people who work with language models and databases, run physics on the GPU in a browser tab, and publish research with the predictions fixed before the data.

about.paragraph: I like software you can run yourself, read end to end and check. Most of what I build is a way to check something: whether a database gives the isolation level it claims, what a power cut leaves on disk, whether two runs of the same model file agree. Before this I worked as a data and ML engineering intern.
facts: A summer 2027 internship or a research spot

wins.what: Won the first ISCJ Hackathon, with my team

research.lead: I work alone, on a laptop, on questions small enough to finish. Each study starts with a file of predictions committed before the first result exists, and the write-up reports every one of them, including the ones that failed.

specimen.heading: Same file, different answers
specimen.text: Same model file, same prompts, greedy decoding. Loading llama.cpp's AVX code path instead of its AVX2 path changed 41 of 600 MMLU answers from Qwen3-0.6B in Q4_K_M. No task's accuracy moved by more than 1.3 points, so a leaderboard would never show it.

ongoing.title: Retry-Storm Stability in Microservice Dependency Graphs
ongoing.sub: A Static, Spectral Bound and Its Limits
ongoing.gist: A bound on how far retries can amplify load across a whole service graph, computed from configuration alone.
body: When a service is overloaded, its callers retry, and the retries add load. Earlier work analyzes this for one service calling another. Real systems are graphs, so I extended the model to any directed dependency graph with a retry budget on every edge, and with circuit breakers as part of the dynamics.

The result is a static check. Build a matrix from routing weights and retry budgets, both of which are in the config before anything is deployed. If its spectral radius is below 1, no load pattern can push any service past a ceiling you can compute. The proof is a Perron-Frobenius monotonicity argument with a Neumann series, the same shape as an epidemic threshold theorem for networks.

I checked the proof three ways: hand-derived fixtures, a second solver written with different numerical methods, and a randomized search of about 5,000 trials that tried to break the bound and did not. Then I looked for where it stops being useful. The bound is tight only when a node is saturated near the boundary. I first guessed that the duration of the surge was what mattered, tested it, and the guess was wrong.

The awkward finding is about real systems. I extracted the call graph of Train-Ticket, a public benchmark with 41 services, and it has no cycles, so its matrix has spectral radius 0 for any retry budget. On that system the theorem holds trivially. The draft says so.

p4c.text: Pages for Change is a student nonprofit in South Brunswick, New Jersey. We collect the children's books families have outgrown, check and log every one, and get them to classrooms, shelters and families. I founded it in 2026 and run the team, the chapters and the book drives. I also built the site and the portal the chapters use to log each book.
p4c.event: Our first event was the Cranbury Community Book Drive on October 24, 2026, run with hearts+homes.
